If you want to get into your dream college, stop trying to copy someone else’s path. It won't get you anywhere. In high school, I authored 5 free math and physics books on my own. I spent thousands of hours, days and nights, building my academy from scratch to help students who couldn’t afford prep materials. Instead of tutoring over Zoom (which a lot of people do), I used writing, something I’m good at, to help in a way that felt authentic to me. That approach got me into multiple of my dream schools, so that's proof doing things slightly differently can work But even more than that: Creating your own path gives you genuine, unique stories to share in your college essays. And the more you your application is, the harder it is to forget. Just because your friend got into UPenn for his ISEF project doesn’t mean qualifying for ISEF will get you there. Just because your friend got into Harvard by starting a nonprofit for special needs kids doesn’t mean you should start the same nonprofit. Do what resonates with you. Don’t be afraid to take the uncommon path. Find a twist on something you care about and go deep with it. It’ll help others. And it’ll help you, more than you think. #T20 #HighSchool #IvyLeague ...more

College apps are brutal as hell. So much of the process is outside your control. That’s why I’m helping you now. The truth is that the game isn't about merit anymore. You can have a 1600 SAT, 4.0 GPA, USAMO medal, ISEF project — and still get rejected. Because now, it’s about how well you craft your story, often appealing to emotion. How you connect your essays, your activities, your voice... specifically for the school you're applying to. What works for CMU, MIT, and Georgia Tech will NOT work for Stanford, Princeton, or Yale. Each school wants different kinds of students. And we know how to speak their language. I almost got suspended for plagiarism in school. I was dishonest, lied to my teacher, and my grade CRASHED. Over 5 years ago in 7th grade, I had a project to write a biography on a famous figure. I chose Einstein. Since I was lazy and wanted the easy way out, I simply copied a source online to write my own text, without realizing the consequences. And obviously, my teacher found out. She called me up and questioned me about this, and I denied it at first. Eventually, I had to admit the truth when I realized there was no way out. I got a zero on the project and an email to my parents that got me grounded for a month. It was a harsh lesson: one about integrity, honesty, and the real cost of shortcuts. I knew that I’d have to be more hardworking starting that day. I thought I was improving my work ethic after that. But fast forward to 2025, and I’m realizing I’m falling into the same trap again. With AI tools like Cursor writing my code, I’m relying too much on shortcuts… letting technology do the thinking for me. Now I feel like the real test is about resisting the easy way out and committing to real growth, even when it’s hard. Because shortcuts might get you through today, but they won’t build the skills you need for tomorrow. Let’s lock in as soon as possible ...more

Today, we're announcing our $4.1 million seed raise for Copperlane (YC W26) . Six months ago, I couldn't have imagined Athan Zhang and I would come this far. I think startups are special in how they reward people that work hard. If you're willing to put twice as much in, you’re able to get more than twice out. Here's what founding Copperlane has taught me: 1. The world is your oyster. When I first moved to SF, I realized how that there was still so much I didn’t know. YC, in particular, showed me that it is possible and that billion dollar companies can be built by two people hacking away in their apartment. Your struggle is real, but you’re not completely insane for thinking it’s possible. 2. Take calculated risks. People generally overestimate the downside and underestimate the upside of starting a company when you’re young. While you shouldn't drop out for the sake of doing so, I believe it’s valid to take calculated risks if there’s a reasonable chance for greater outcomes. 3. The joy is in the journey. At some point or another, when everything goes wrong, you’ll be forced to think hard on why you want to be a founder. When people ask, I still can’t exactly put into words why I chose to do so. Part of it is the freedom, the other part is just the amazing process and personal journey it takes you on. Thanks to our early believers ( Y Combinator , TQ Ventures , Harshita Arora , and more), customers (you know who you are), and friends. Always so grateful for this privilege to build. Now back to work. ❤️ P.S. We are growing quickly and hiring. DM or email brianna@copperlane.ai if you want to join a winning team. https://lnkd.in/eMHY_A_C

Life comes full circle. The American Water Resources Association recently reached out to publish some research I did on advanced techniques for satellite based remote monitoring of water volumes in water bodies. My work included triaging satellite streams, correcting for cloud cover, seeing past surface vegetation, and accounting for artificial pollutants. Through previous experience I had with building around Water-Tech, I developed a personal validation gate to deploy any pipeline I built on a specific reservoir at the foothills of the Himalayas: one that governed water access to millions. Tehri reservoir. When I shared the publication on my family group chat I saw a heartwarming reply from my mother (who had no idea about the research I was conducting) saying that my great grandfather was a part of the team that engineered Tehri reservoir. I immediately lit up. As a CS student building at the frontier of AI, changing water infrastructure is as far as it gets from my typical trajectory. The opportunities we get are presented to us for a reason, it’s important that we seize each one.

Worlds-qualified in 2025 and 2026, finishing this season ranked #90 in the world out of 3,900 teams. • AI research published at ICML workshops on LLM-based ad rewriting • Research at UC Santa Cruz (autonomous vehicle sensor fusion) and SJSU's Library Technology Integration Lab (sign language recognition for accessible educational technology) • NCWIT Aspirations in Computing, Bay Area Regional Winner • Co-founder & Director of Milpitas Hacks, a hackathon bringing together students across the Bay Area • Girl Scout Gold Award: STEM with Kindness, designing and running inclusive robotics workshops for students with disabilities through FCSN • MUSD Girls Who Code Summer Camp, reaching 200+ K-8 students yearly, including from 5 Title I schools What I'm most proud of isn't any one project.
